blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Correlated Ensemble Failures**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Multi-Agent Coordination, § Correlated Ensemble Failures
blocks.md: Adding a panel of five model reviewers to `migration_task_01` to check semantic correctness before publication exposes the same shared-assumption hazard. All five reviewers may endorse `worker_caller_01`'s patch because they share the mistaken assumption that the legacy interface remains available, accumulating approvals without ever verifying the underlying dependency. This synchronized breakdown illustrates a **correlated failure**, in which the reviewers fail on the same inputs. When individual agents share systemic blind spots, consensus among them is informative only up to the limits of their joint error distribution.

blocks.title: What the section covers

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Correlated reviewers matters for the system this section describes.

questions.q: The section **Correlated Ensemble Failures** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A credit window enforces free plus outstanding equal to W, bounding in-flight payload and, by Little's law, mean staleness at W/mu, which per-agent token budgets cannot do.
Reviewers share each candidate's difficulty, so correlated errors set an irreducible floor on majority-vote false approval that adding reviewers cannot remove.

A delegated worker owns a separate child trajectory, and a capable single controller already runs tools and candidates concurrently, so delegation buys only separation of context, authority, and lifecycle, at the price of new boundaries.

A typed task envelope binds a child to immutable inputs, a scoped grant, a reservation, and required evidence that the runtime resolves, and the receipt carries runtime-populated evidence back, so a worker cannot widen either.
